text: The derivative says that a smooth curve, seen up close, looks like a straight line. Taylor series turn that observation into a tool: approximate a complicated function near a point with simple polynomials, and keep adding terms until the approximation is as good as you need.

The first approximation is the tangent line itself. Near a point a, the value of f at x is close to the value at a, plus the slope times the distance from a. For the exponential function near zero, that gives one plus x, which is excellent for small x but drifts away as you move further out, because a straight line cannot bend.

To capture the bending, add a term in the square of the distance, scaled by half the second derivative, which measures how fast the slope itself is changing. The tangent line becomes a parabola that hugs the curve over a wider stretch, curving the same way the function does.

Each further term matches one more derivative at the point, and the term with the n-th power is divided by n factorial. For the exponential, every derivative at zero equals one, so the series is one plus x, plus x squared over two, plus x cubed over six, and so on, and with enough terms it reproduces e to the x everywhere.

The sine function makes a good show. Its series has only odd powers, and you can watch the polynomials wrap themselves around more and more of its waves before peeling away. Close to the point, a few terms are plenty; far away you need many, and for some functions the series never reaches beyond a certain distance at all.

Optimisers live on the first two terms. Gradient descent trusts the linear term, which is only accurate near the current point, and that is why it takes small steps. Methods that also use the second derivative, the curvature, model the loss as a parabola and jump towards its bottom, which is the idea behind Newton's method.

Every training step of a language model is a bet on the first order approximation: it assumes the loss changes linearly for a small move of the weights, a bet that only pays off if the learning rate keeps the step small. That completes calculus. Next, module three begins with random variables and distributions.
